message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This analysis cuts through a lot of anecdote about churn and shows exactly where it is happening. We segmented the whole residential base by contract status, using a full six months of billing data rather than a sample, and combined that with the reasons customers gave when they left. The picture is clear. Churn is low in contract and rises sharply afterwards, and it is highest among customers who have been out of contract for more than a year, so that is where the retention offer is aimed. The reasons data confirm that price is the main driver, and the May spike after the price rise reinforces this. We have also put a clear number on what is at stake, around £7.4 million a year in lost revenue, which puts the cost of the proposed offer into perspective. The recommendations are targeted and affordable, and I am confident they focus our H2 retention budget where it will make the most difference.
</author>

<document>
Customer Churn Analysis: Residential Broadband, H1 2026
Customer Insight Team, Brightline Fibre, July 2026

1. Purpose
This analysis examines residential broadband churn in the first half of 2026, identifies where it is concentrated, and recommends where retention spending should be focused in H2. Churn is our largest single driver of revenue loss and acquisition cost: each lost customer costs around £180 to replace through marketing and installation.

2. Context
Brightline applied an annual price rise of 6.5% to all residential broadband customers in April 2026, in line with the terms of their contracts. Two national competitors launched aggressive introductory offers in the same quarter. Our minimum contract term for new customers is 18 months; after that, customers roll onto a monthly contract at the same price and can leave with 30 days' notice.

Churn in this analysis means customers whose broadband service ended during the period. Customers who moved to another Brightline product, such as a business or mobile-bundle tariff, and customers who moved home and transferred their service within our network, are not counted as churn. Customer numbers are taken from the billing system at 1 January.

3. Churn by contract status
Table 1. Residential broadband churn, 1 January to 30 June 2026
Segment | Customers at 1 January | Churned in H1 | H1 churn rate
In minimum term | 182,000 | 5,460 | 3.0%
Out of contract, less than 12 months | 64,000 | 7,040 | 11.0%
Out of contract, 12 months or more | 48,000 | 3,840 | 8.0%
Total | 294,000 | 16,340 | 5.6%

Churn is low among customers in their minimum term, as expected, because leaving early incurs a charge. Once out of contract, churn rises sharply. It is highest among our longest-standing out-of-contract customers, those who have been out of contract for 12 months or more, who appear to accumulate dissatisfaction with paying full price over time.

Table 2. Reasons given at cancellation (H1 2026, where recorded)
Reason | Share
Price / found a cheaper deal | 46%
Moving home | 21%
Service reliability | 14%
Customer service experience | 9%
Other | 10%

Price was the dominant reason, cited by almost half of leavers. Cancellations peaked in May, the month after the price rise, when 3,620 customers left, compared with a monthly average of about 2,540 in the rest of the half-year.

4. Revenue impact
Average revenue per customer is £34 a month. The 16,340 customers lost in H1 therefore represent annualised revenue of about £7.4 million, before the cost of replacing them.

5. Recommendations
5.1 Target a proactive retention offer at customers who have been out of contract for 12 months or more, since this is where churn is highest. The offer would be a 10% discount in return for a new 12-month commitment. There are 48,000 such customers, and the discount would cost about £2.0 million a year if all accepted; in practice we expect take-up of around 40%.
5.2 Review the timing and communication of future annual price rises. The spike in cancellations after the 8% April price rise suggests that customers were not adequately prepared, and that clearer advance communication could reduce price-driven churn.
5.3 Investigate the reliability complaints, which are concentrated in three exchange areas.
5.4 Report churn monthly by segment to the Commercial Committee from September, so that the effect of the retention offer can be tracked.

6. Conclusion
Churn is concentrated among long-standing out-of-contract customers and is primarily price-driven. A targeted retention offer to this group, together with better price-rise communication, is the most effective use of our H2 retention budget.
</document>
response:
# Review: Customer Churn Analysis, Residential Broadband H1 2026

The data and structure are sound, but the main recommendation contradicts the document's own table. Two other figures are also wrong, and the conclusion should not go forward as written.

## Critical issues

**1. The targeting recommendation contradicts Table 1.**
The text, conclusion and Recommendation 5.1 all say churn is highest among customers out of contract for 12 months or more. Table 1 shows the opposite:

| Segment | Churn rate | Customers lost |
|---|---|---|
| Out of contract, <12 months | **11.0%** | **7,040** |
| Out of contract, 12+ months | 8.0% | 3,840 |

The less-than-12-months group is the worst segment by rate and by volume. It accounts for 43% of all H1 churn from 22% of the base. The explanation that customers "accumulate dissatisfaction over time" is not supported. A more likely reading is that price-sensitive customers leave soon after their contract ends, and those still with us after a year are less likely to go.

As written, the offer is aimed at the wrong group. The analysis points to intervening at or just before the end of the minimum term, the point where churn jumps from 3% to 11%.

**2. The revenue figure is overstated.**
16,340 × £34 × 12 = **£6.67m**, not £7.4m. £7.4m would need about 18,100 leavers. The label also needs care. This is the annual revenue of customers lost in H1. It is not a full-year churn cost, which would be roughly double. It also isn't revenue actually lost in H1, because leavers churned throughout the period.

**3. The price rise is given as two different figures.**
Section 2 says 6.5%; Recommendation 5.2 says 8%. One is wrong, and this matters in a document arguing that price drives churn.

## Significant issues

**4. The retention offer's economics are incomplete.**
The £2.0m cost (48,000 × £34 × 12 × 10%) is correct, and 40% take-up gives about £0.8m. But H1 churn in this group was 8%, so roughly 84% of the group would likely stay for the year anyway. Most of the discount would go to customers who were never going to leave. The paper needs a break-even estimate: how many leavers must be retained to cover the discount, compared with the £180 replacement cost and lost margin. The same test should be run for the <12-month group, where more of the spend would reach likely leavers.

**5. Segments are fixed at 1 January.**
Customers change segment during the half-year. In-term customers reach the end of their term, and <12-month customers cross into 12+. Churn is attributed to each customer's segment on 1 January, not their status when they left. This probably understates churn at the contract-expiry point, which strengthens issue 1. Assigning segment at the date of churn would be more accurate.

**6. The reasons data do not support targeting by segment.**
- Table 2 is not broken down by contract status, so it cannot show that the 12+ group is especially price-driven.
- "Where recorded" needs a coverage rate. If many leavers have no reason recorded, the 46% may not be representative.
- "Moving home" (21%) is mostly churn the company cannot prevent. Excluding it would make the price share larger and give a clearer view of churn that can be addressed.

**7. The May spike has more than one possible cause.**
Competitors launched aggressive offers in the same quarter, so the spike cannot be attributed to the price rise alone. The 30-day notice period would also push April decisions into May exits. Splitting the May cancellations by segment and by reason would help separate these causes. The arithmetic itself checks out: 3,620 plus 5 × ~2,544 ≈ 16,340.

## Minor issues

- **Rec 5.2** says customers "were not adequately prepared," but no evidence about communication is presented. It reads as an assumption.
- **Rec 5.3** mentions three exchange areas, but no reliability data appear in the document. Add a table or a reference.
- Replacement cost could be quantified in the same way as revenue: 16,340 × £180 ≈ **£2.9m**.
- Consider whether a 12-month recommitment is the right length, given the 18-month standard term.
- The paper is dated July and aimed at the H2 budget. If it is being reviewed now (November), the timing and the September reporting start in 5.4 need updating.

## On the author's summary

The summary repeats the central error. It says churn is "highest among customers who have been out of contract for more than a year," but the table shows it isn't. The summary also says the reasons data "confirm" the targeting, when they don't address segments at all. The use of full billing data rather than a sample is a real strength. The underlying numbers are internally consistent. The problems are in how they have been interpreted.

## Suggested fixes before circulation

1. Rewrite Section 3's interpretation, Rec 5.1 and the Conclusion to reflect that churn peaks in the first year out of contract.
2. Correct the revenue figure to about £6.7m and clarify what it represents.
3. Make the price-rise percentage consistent.
4. Add a break-even analysis for the offer, covering both out-of-contract segments.
5. Break down reasons and the May spike by segment, and state how many leavers had a reason recorded.
